title: How a Text Is Built
bigQuestion: How does knowing the shape of a text help you understand and remember it?

story.title: Two Articles, One Tornado
story.kicker: One article tells what happened minute by minute. The other tells why the sky turned. Same storm, two shapes.
paragraphs: A tornado touched down west of a small Illinois town on a June afternoon. The next week, Ms. Okafor's class got two articles about it. "Read both," she said. "Then tell me how they are different." Priya read the first one. It felt like a movie.

The first article began at 3:10 p.m., when the sky went green. At 3:25 the sirens went off. At 3:40 the funnel touched a cornfield. At 3:52 it lifted. The article walked through the storm one minute at a time. Priya could almost hear the clock ticking.

The second article did not have a single clock time in it. It started with warm, wet air from the south. It said the warm air met cool, dry air from the north. The warm air rose, the storm began to spin, and the spin tightened into a funnel. Every sentence answered the question why.

"The first one is a sequence," Priya said. "First, next, then. The second one is cause and effect. This happens, so that happens." Ms. Okafor wrote both words on the board. "Two writers. Same tornado. Two shapes," she said.

Then she asked the class to take notes on each. For the first article, Priya drew a line with times on it. For the second, she drew arrows: warm air meets cold air, arrow, air rises, arrow, spin, arrow, funnel. Her notes looked like the articles. That was the whole point.
story.think: Priya's notes for each article had a different shape. Why would a line work for one and arrows for the other?

lessons.title: Sequence and Description
lessons.mainIdea: A sequence text tells events or steps in order, and a description text tells what something is like, feature by feature.
reading: Read this. "First, the sky turned green. Next, the sirens sounded. Then the funnel touched down. Finally, it lifted." Each event comes after the one before. This is a *sequence* text. Recipes, directions, and the story of a day are all sequences. Order is the whole point.

Now read this. "A tornado is a spinning column of air. It reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. It can be thin as a rope or wider than a town. Most last only a few minutes." Nothing happens in order here. Each sentence adds a feature. This is a *description* text. It tells what something is like.

How do you tell them apart? Ask, "Could I shuffle these sentences?" In a sequence, no. Mixing the order breaks it. In a description, mostly yes. The tornado is still a spinning column even if you read the width sentence first. Every text you read has a shape. Sequence and description are the first two.

words.d: a text shape that tells events or steps in time order
a text shape that tells what something is like, one feature at a time
the way a text is built or organized

look.title: Shuffle Test
look.text: Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake that lies entirely inside the United States. Its water is cold even in July. Its beaches in Chicago have soft sand. On a clear day the water looks blue-green near the shore.
look.prompt: Could you shuffle these sentences without breaking the paragraph? What shape is it?

check.q: Which shape puts events in time order?
check.why: Sequence means first, next, then. Order is the point.

check.q: "A tornado can be thin as a rope or wider than a town." What kind of sentence is this?
check.why: It tells what a tornado is like, one feature. That is description.

check.q: What does the shuffle test show?
choices: Sequence sentences can be mixed; description cannot
Both shapes can be mixed freely
Description sentences can mostly be mixed; sequence cannot
check.why: Mixing steps breaks a sequence. Mixing features usually leaves a description fine.

lessons.title: Compare and Contrast
lessons.mainIdea: A compare-and-contrast text shows how two things are alike and how they are different.
reading: "A tornado and a hurricane both spin. Both can flatten houses. But a hurricane is hundreds of miles wide and lasts for days. A tornado is usually less than a mile wide and lasts minutes." This paragraph holds two things side by side. That is *compare and contrast*.

To *compare* is to show what is the same. To *contrast* is to show what is different. Watch the words. "Both" and "also" and "alike" signal same. "But," "however," "while" and "unlike" signal different. Writers use these words like turn signals.

Try it on two things you know: a bus and a train. Both carry many people. Both have a driver. But a train runs on rails and a bus runs on streets. A train cannot turn to avoid traffic. When you can say both and but, you are thinking in this shape.

words.d: to show how two things are alike
to show how two things are different
a huge spinning storm that forms over warm ocean water and can last for days

look.title: Tornado and Hurricane Side by Side
look.cite: rounded, typical values chosen for this lesson; real storms vary a lot
look.prompt: Which numbers show a contrast? Name one way the two storms are alike that the table does not show.

check.q: What does contrast mean?
check.why: Contrast is difference. Compare is sameness.

check.q: Which word signals that two things are alike?
check.why: "Both" says two things share something. The others signal difference.

check.q: Which sentence is a contrast between a bus and a train?
choices: A train runs on rails, but a bus runs on streets
check.why: The "but" sentence shows a difference. The other three show sameness.

lessons.title: Cause and Effect
lessons.mainIdea: A cause-and-effect text explains why something happens: this cause leads to that effect.
reading: The second tornado article answered one question over and over: why? "Warm, wet air pushed north. Cool, dry air pushed south. Where they met, the warm air rose fast. Because the winds blew at different speeds, the rising air began to spin." Each sentence is a *cause* pushing an *effect*.

A cause is the reason. An effect is the result. Watch for "because," "so," "since," "as a result" and "led to." Also watch for chains. Warm air rising causes spin. Spin causes a funnel. The funnel causes damage. One effect becomes the next cause.

Here is a trap. Two things happening close together does not mean one caused the other. The sirens sounded, and then the funnel touched down. The sirens did not cause the tornado. Ask, "Did the first thing make the second thing happen?" If not, it is a sequence, not a cause.

words.d: the reason something happens
the result; what happens because of a cause
a line of causes and effects where each effect starts the next cause

look.title: Is It a Cause?
look.text: Read two pairs. Pair one: "The pond froze, so the ducks left." Pair two: "The bell rang, and then it started to snow." In the first pair, the freezing pond took away the ducks' food and swimming water. In the second, the bell and the snow just happened close in time.
look.prompt: Which pair is cause and effect? Which is only a sequence? How do you know?

check.q: In "the warm air rose, so the storm began to spin," what is the effect?
check.why: The spinning is the result. The rising warm air is the cause.

check.q: What is a chain of causes?
choices: Two things that happen at the same time
A line where each effect starts the next cause
check.why: Rising air causes spin, spin causes a funnel, the funnel causes damage. Each effect leads to the next.

check.q: The sirens sounded, then the funnel touched down. Did the sirens cause the funnel?
choices: No; they just happened close in time
Yes; the first thing always causes the second
check.why: Close in time is not the same as cause. The sirens did not make the tornado happen.

lessons.title: Problem and Solution
lessons.mainIdea: A problem-and-solution text names something wrong and then tells how people fixed it or could fix it.
reading: "Tornado sirens are loud, but people inside cannot always hear them. So the town added phone alerts. Now a warning buzzes in every pocket." First a *problem*. Then a *solution*. This shape shows up in science, history and the news all the time.

Watch for "problem," "trouble," "issue" and "the challenge was." Then watch for "solved," "fixed," "one answer" and "so they." Sometimes a text gives more than one solution. Sometimes it gives a solution that failed and then a better one. Keep track of which is which.

This shape is close to cause and effect, and students mix them up. Ask, "Is the writer telling me what went wrong and how to fix it?" That is problem and solution. "Is the writer telling me why something happens?" That is cause and effect. A problem is a kind of cause, but only one that someone tries to fix.

words.d: something wrong that needs to be fixed
a way to fix a problem

look.title: A Town Fixes a Problem
look.text: After the storm, the town had one shelter, and it was two miles from the school. Kids could never reach it in time. The school board voted to build a storm room inside the school itself. It has thick concrete walls and no windows. Now every student is thirty seconds from safety.
look.prompt: Name the problem and the solution. What words helped you find each?

check.q: "People could not hear the sirens, so the town added phone alerts." What shape is this?
check.why: Something was wrong (no one heard), and the town fixed it (phone alerts).

check.q: In the shelter story, what is the solution?
choices: The shelter was two miles away
A storm room inside the school
Kids could not reach the shelter
check.why: The storm room is the fix. The far-away shelter is the problem.

check.q: How is problem and solution different from cause and effect?
choices: Problem and solution has no reasons
Cause and effect only happens in stories
Problem and solution tells how something wrong gets fixed
check.why: Cause and effect explains why. Problem and solution adds a fix.

lessons.title: Words That Give Away the Shape
lessons.mainIdea: Signal words like first, both, because and solved tell you which structure a text is using before you finish it.
reading: Read just the first few words of a paragraph: "First, crack two eggs." You already know it is a sequence. "Unlike a frog, a toad..." Compare and contrast. "Because the river flooded..." Cause and effect. "The trouble with old bridges is..." Problem and solution. These are *signal words*. They give away the shape early.

Learn a few for each shape. Sequence: first, next, then, after, finally, dates and clock times. Description: for example, such as, looks like, is made of. Compare and contrast: both, also, alike, but, however, unlike. Cause and effect: because, so, since, as a result. Problem and solution: problem, trouble, so they, solved, one answer.

Signal words are clues, not proof. A description might use "first" just to start a list of features. So read a little more and check. If the sentences must stay in order, it is a sequence. If they explain why, it is cause and effect. The signal word points; the sentences tell.

words.d: a word or phrase that hints at how a text is organized, like first, but or because
a hint that helps you figure something out

look.title: Signal Words in the Two Tornado Articles
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in two model articles written for this course
look.prompt: Which counts point to sequence? Which point to cause and effect? Could you tell the shape from the counts alone?

check.q: A paragraph begins, "Because the river flooded..." Which shape is most likely?
check.why: "Because" signals a cause is coming.

check.q: Which set of words signals a sequence?
check.why: First, next and finally put events in order.

check.q: Why are signal words clues and not proof?
choices: A word like first can start a list of features, not just steps
check.why: Signal words point to a shape, but you must read on to be sure.

lessons.title: Notes That Match the Shape
lessons.mainIdea: Take notes in the shape of the text: a numbered list for sequence, a two-column chart for compare and contrast, arrows for cause and effect.
reading: Priya drew a line with times for the first article. She drew arrows for the second. Her notes matched the shape of each text. That is not a trick. It is the best way to remember. When your notes look like the text, your brain stores the ideas the way the writer built them.

Here is the plan. Sequence: a numbered list or a timeline. Description: a web, with the topic in the middle and features around it. Compare and contrast: two columns, or two circles that overlap. Cause and effect: boxes with arrows. Problem and solution: one box for the problem, one for each fix.

Try it with the shelter paragraph. Problem box: "Shelter two miles away; kids cannot reach it." Solution box: "Storm room inside school, concrete walls." Two boxes, ten words. You could tell the whole story from that. Notes that match the shape are short, and they stick.

words.d: a line with events marked on it in time order
a note shape with the topic in the middle and features drawn around it
a tall list; two columns side by side let you compare

look.title: Pick the Note Shape
look.text: Three students each read a different article. Amir's article explains why leaves turn red in fall. Beth's article compares two kinds of bridges. Carlos's article gives the steps to plant a tree. Amir draws two columns. Beth draws arrows. Carlos draws a web.
look.prompt: All three picked the wrong note shape. What should each student have drawn instead?

check.q: Which note shape fits a cause-and-effect text?
check.why: Arrows show one thing leading to another, which is what cause and effect does.

check.q: Beth's article compares two bridges. What should she draw?
check.why: Two columns put the two bridges side by side so she can compare and contrast.

check.q: Why do notes that match the shape help you remember?
choices: They store the ideas the way the writer built them
check.why: When your notes copy the structure, the ideas stick in that same order.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Texts
lessons.mainIdea: When two texts cover the same topic, compare what each one includes, what each leaves out, and how each is built.
reading: The two tornado articles covered the same storm. But they did not say the same things. The first had clock times and no reasons. The second had reasons and no clock times. Reading both, Priya knew more than she could learn from either one alone. That is why teachers give you two texts.

To compare two texts, ask three questions. What facts are in both? What facts are only in one? How is each text built? Make two columns. Put shared facts in the middle. Put the facts only in the first text on the left, and only in the second on the right.

Then ask why. Why did the first writer leave out the causes? Maybe she wanted readers to feel the minutes tick. Why did the second writer skip the clock? Maybe he wanted to teach the science. Each writer chose. Seeing the choice is the deepest kind of reading.

words.d: to put something in; a text includes the facts the writer chose to keep
to not put something in; every writer leaves out some facts

look.title: What Each Article Kept
look.text: Article 1 has: the sky turning green at 3:10, the sirens at 3:25, the funnel at 3:40, the lift at 3:52, the flattened barn. Article 2 has: warm wet air from the south, cool dry air from the north, rising air, winds at different speeds, the spin, the funnel, the flattened barn.
look.prompt: Which fact is in both articles? What is one thing you would know only from Article 2?

check.q: Why read two texts on the same topic?
choices: To learn more than either one alone gives
check.why: Each text includes different facts. Together they give a fuller picture.

check.q: Which fact was in both tornado articles?
check.why: Only the barn appears in both lists. The others are in just one article.

check.q: What is the deepest question to ask about two texts?
choices: Why did each writer choose to include what they did?
check.why: Seeing the writer's choices shows you the purpose behind each text.

lessons.title: The Author's Point and Reasons
lessons.mainIdea: An author often makes a point and gives reasons for it; your job is to find the point and check whether the reasons really hold it up.
reading: Some texts do more than tell. They argue. "Every school in Illinois should have a storm room. Tornadoes hit our state every year. Kids cannot reach a shelter two miles away. A storm room costs less than one school bus." The first sentence is the author's *point*. The next three are the *reasons*.

Find the point first. It is usually a sentence with "should," "must," "best" or "most important." Then find each reason. Ask, "Does this reason really hold up the point?" "Tornadoes hit every year" holds it up. "Storm rooms are painted gray" would not. A point with weak reasons is a weak point.

Then count. One reason is thin. Three good reasons with a fact for each is strong. Also notice what the author does not say. The storm-room author never mentions who pays. A careful reader sees the point, checks the reasons, and notices the hole.

words.d: the thing an author is trying to convince you of
a fact or idea an author gives to hold up a point

look.title: Find the Point
look.text: Chicago should plant more trees along its streets. Trees give shade, and shaded streets stay cooler in July. Tree roots soak up rain, so there is less water in the sewers after a storm. And a block with trees just looks like a place people care about.
look.prompt: What is the point? Which reason is the strongest, and which is the weakest? Why?

check.q: Which sentence is the author's point?
choices: Tornadoes hit our state every year
Every school in Illinois should have a storm room
A storm room costs less than a bus
Kids cannot reach a shelter two miles away
check.why: The point has "should" and is what the other sentences hold up.

check.q: Which reason would NOT hold up the storm-room point?
choices: Kids cannot reach the far shelter
It costs less than a bus
check.why: Paint color has nothing to do with whether schools need a storm room.

check.q: What hole does the careful reader find in the storm-room argument?
choices: It never says when tornadoes happen
It never says how big a storm room is
check.why: The author gives a cost but never says who would pay it.

lessons.title: Reading Science and History
lessons.mainIdea: A science text is usually built on causes, steps and diagrams, while a history text is built on dates, people and reasons, so read each with a different set of questions.
reading: A science text about tornadoes asks, "How does this work?" It is full of causes, steps and diagrams. Read it slowly. Check every diagram against the words. Ask, "Could I explain this to a friend with my hands?" If the text says warm air rises, picture it rising.

A history text about a tornado asks, "What happened to people, and why did it matter?" It has dates, names and places. It tells what people did before and after. Read it asking, "Who is telling this? What did they see? What changed because of it?"

One real storm, the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925, crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana and was one of the deadliest in United States history. A science text about it would explain the air and the spin. A history text would tell about the towns and the people who rebuilt. Same storm, different questions, different reading.

words.d: the story of what happened to people in the past
a text that explains how something in nature works
to build again after something was destroyed

look.title: Two Questions for One Storm
look.text: Imagine two books open on a desk. The left page shows a diagram: warm air, cold air, rising arrows, a spinning column. The right page shows a photo of a town's main street after the 1925 storm and a paragraph about neighbors sharing food. A student reads the left page with her hands moving. She reads the right page asking who these people were.
look.prompt: Which page is science and which is history? What question fits each one?

check.q: What question does a science text mostly answer?
check.why: Science texts explain how nature works, with causes, steps and diagrams.

check.q: Which parts would you expect most in a history text?
check.why: History tells what happened to people, so it is full of dates, names and places.

check.q: The Tri-State Tornado of 1925 crossed which three states?
check.why: It crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, which is why it is called Tri-State.

lessons.title: Timelines and Steps
lessons.mainIdea: Timelines and numbered steps are sequences drawn out, so read them left to right or top to bottom and check the spacing between events.
reading: A *timeline* is a sequence you can see. Events sit on a line, earliest on the left, latest on the right. Priya's tornado timeline had 3:10, 3:25, 3:40 and 3:52. The spaces between the marks matter. The gap from 3:10 to 3:25 is fifteen minutes. From 3:40 to 3:52 is twelve. You can read time with your eyes.

Numbered *steps* are a sequence too. "1. Go to the lowest floor. 2. Get away from windows. 3. Cover your head." Read them in order. Do not skip. Step three makes no sense if you have not done step one. When steps have pictures, match each picture to its number before you move on.

Both tools can hide gaps. A timeline of a town might jump from 1925 to 1950. Ask what happened in between. A recipe might say "bake" without saying for how long. Good readers notice what a timeline or a list of steps leaves out, and they ask.

words.d: the parts of a task done one after another, usually numbered
a space or a missing part between two things

look.title: Minutes Between the Marks
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the clock times in the class story
look.prompt: Which gap was shortest? How long was the tornado on the ground?

check.q: On a timeline, where is the earliest event?
check.why: Timelines run left to right, earliest to latest.

check.q: Why should you read numbered steps in order?
choices: The numbers are the hard part
Later steps depend on earlier ones
The last step is always first
Order does not matter for steps
check.why: Step three makes no sense if step one is not done.

check.q: A timeline jumps from 1925 to 1950. What should a good reader do?
choices: Ask what happened in the gap
check.why: Timelines can leave things out. Noticing the gap is part of reading it.

review.q: The first tornado article walked through the storm minute by minute. What is its shape?
review.why: Events in time order with clock times is a sequence.

review.q: The second article explained why the storm formed. What is its shape?
review.why: Every sentence answered why, with one thing leading to the next.

review.q: Which shape can usually pass the shuffle test?
review.why: Features can be read in almost any order. Steps and causes cannot.

review.q: "Unlike a bus, a train runs on rails." What does "unlike" signal?
review.why: "Unlike" points to a difference between two things.

review.q: What is the best note shape for compare and contrast?
review.why: Two columns put two things side by side.

review.q: A writer gives a point and one reason. Another gives the same point with three reasons and a fact for each. Which argument is stronger?
choices: The one with three reasons and facts
review.why: More good reasons with facts hold up the point better.

review.q: What is the trap in cause and effect?
choices: Thinking two things close in time must be cause and effect
review.why: The sirens came before the funnel, but they did not cause it.

review.q: What happens when your notes match the text's shape?
choices: You do not need to read
The teacher writes them for you
review.why: Notes built like the text store the ideas the way the writer built them.
